# 6. Cell visualization

**Module 06 — Cell visualization.** 2D and 3D single-cell graph plots using
pixelatorR's `cell_plot` visualization framework. This shows *where* proteins sit on a
single cell's surface graph (clustering, polarization and colocalization patterns
that population-level scores in module `04` summarise but don't show directly). Run
after module `02`. See the [cell visualization tutorial](https://software.pixelgen.com/pna-analysis/R/tutorials/cell_visualization/)
for more detail.

```{r}
#| label: module06b_setup

library(here)
here::i_am("modules/06_cell_visualization.qmd")

source(here::here("modules", "common_setup.R"))

if (!exists("pg_data", inherits = TRUE)) {
  pg_data <- load_checkpoint("annotated_seurat_object.rds")
}
```

## 6.1. Parameters

> **Decision checkpoint** (set the cell type and markers to plot). 
> In practice, cell visualization is an interactive process, where you select cells and markers of interest based on prior knowledge and/or analysis results and then plot them - often in multiple ways. The example presented here uses CD8 T cells and the CD82/CD81 pair, which often colocalize on the cell surface. 

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_parameters

cell_type_of_interest <- "CD8 T"           # one value from `cell_annotation`
markers_to_viz        <- c("CD82", "CD81") # pair inspected for colocalization
n_cells               <- 4                 # cells in the grid and the grid animation
# Grey background nodes, one color per marker in `markers_to_viz`
marker_colors <- c(Other = "grey85", CD82 = "#E53E3E", CD81 = "#3182BD")
light_direction <- c(-1, 0.5, 1)           # shared lighting for the static renders
out_dir <- here::here("results/06_cell_visualization")
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## 6.2. Select cells

How you pick cells depends on what you want to show — the spatial pattern on typical cells, a
polarized marker, a colocalization pattern, or a cell–cell conjugate. In this example, we rank cells of the chosen type by the colocalization `log2_ratio` of the marker pair, and keep those with enough observed joins that the ratio is meaningful and interesting to visualize.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_select_cells

# Sample `n_cells` cells from the cells of interest
sel_cells <- pg_data |>
  subset(cell_annotation == cell_type_of_interest) |>
  ProximityScores(lazy = TRUE) |>
  filter(
    marker_1 %in% markers_to_viz,
    marker_2 %in% markers_to_viz,
    marker_1 != marker_2
  ) |>
  filter(join_count > 100) |>
  arrange(desc(log2_ratio)) |>
  collect() |>
  slice_head(n = n_cells)

cells_of_interest <- sel_cells$component
if (length(cells_of_interest) == 0) {
  stop("No '", cell_type_of_interest, "' cells pass the selection filter.")
}
```

## 6.3. Load graphs, layouts, and local proximity scores

In this step we load the cell graphs into the Seurat object, compute the layouts using one of several supported algorithms, and compute the local proximity scores for the selected cells. For this last step, we use `ComputeLPS()` to write one score per node per marker. The default call stores self-clustering of each marker into the `lps` layer. The second call to `ComputeLPS()`, with `mode = "all"`, stores one colocalization score for the pair into the `coloc` layer; a single vector is saved as node metadata named `coloc`.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_layout

pg_data <- RemoveCellGraphs(pg_data)
pg_data <- pg_data |>
  LoadCellGraphs(cells = cells_of_interest) |>
  ComputeLayout(layout_method = "spectral") |>
  ComputeLPS(markers = markers_to_viz) |> # Compute local proximity scores for each marker
  ComputeLPS(markers = markers_to_viz, mode = "all", name = "coloc") # Compute local proximity score for the pair
```

## 6.4. Fetch layout data

In this step we extract the layout data for the selected cells and associated metadata layers which we than can use to annotate and visualize the data. We create two data frames, one from the `counts` layer and one from the `lps` and `coloc` layers. The `counts` layer carries the node identity (`marker`) used for overlays. The `lps` layer carries per-marker local proximity scores. The `coloc` layer carries the local proximity score for the pair. We than transfer the `coloc` column to the `lps` layer to create a single data frame with all the scores. Both objects have the same node order, so binding the `coloc` column by position keeps each score on its node.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_layout_data

layout_counts <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cells_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = markers_to_viz,
  add_marker = TRUE,
  layer = "counts"
)

layout_lps <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cells_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = markers_to_viz,
  layer = "lps"
)
layout_coloc <- FetchLayoutData(
  pg_data,
  cells = cells_of_interest,
  layout_method = "spectral_3d",
  vars = "coloc"
)
layout_lps <- bind_cols(layout_lps, layout_coloc |> select(coloc))
```

## 6.5. Single cell, one marker

A 2D projection of one cell. We can plot the counts layer to highlight the individual CD82 proteins on the cell surface and the LPS layer to highlight the CD82 clustering on the cell surface. Depth and directional light make near and far nodes create a more realistic 3D appearance without an interactive viewer.
We also add a title and legend to the plots.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_single_marker

# Plot the counts layer to highlight the CD82 protein on the cell surface
p_counts <- layout_counts |>
  filter(component == cells_of_interest[1]) |>
  cell_plot(color = CD82, size = 0.7) |>
  cell_node_depth(focal_distance = 1.8) |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction) |>
  cell_annotation(
    title = paste(cell_type_of_interest, "—", cells_of_interest[1]),
    legend_title = "CD82"
  )

export_plot(filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(cell_type_of_interest, "_", cells_of_interest[1], "_counts.png")), plot = autoplot(p_counts))

# Plot the LPS layer to highlight the CD82 clustering on the cell surface
p_lps <- layout_lps |>
  filter(component == cells_of_interest[1]) |>
  cell_plot(color = CD82, size = 0.7) |>
  cell_node_scale_color() |>
  cell_node_depth(focal_distance = 1.8) |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction) |>
  cell_annotation(
    title = paste(cell_type_of_interest, "—", cells_of_interest[1]),
    legend_title = "CD82 LPS"
  )
  
export_plot(filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(cell_type_of_interest, "_", cells_of_interest[1], "_lps.png")), plot = autoplot(p_lps))
```

## 6.6. Single cell, multi-marker overlay

We can also plot several markers on the same cell to visualize their spatial pattern on the same cell. Here we use the `counts` object to highlight the individual CD82 and CD81 proteins on the cell surface.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_multi_marker

p_multi_marker <- layout_counts |>
  filter(component == cells_of_interest[1]) |>
  mutate(
    marker = if_else(marker %in% markers_to_viz, marker, "Other"),
    highlight = as.numeric(marker != "Other")
  ) |>
  cell_plot(color = marker, size = highlight, alpha = highlight) |>
  cell_node_scale_color(colors = marker_colors) |>
  cell_node_scale_size(sizes = c(0.4, 3)) |>
  cell_node_scale_alpha(alphas = c(0.5, 1))

export_plot(filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(cell_type_of_interest, "_", cells_of_interest[1], "_multi_marker.png")), plot = autoplot(p_multi_marker))
```

## 6.7. Single cell, local proximity panels

We can also plot the local proximity scores for the individual markers and the pair on the same cell.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_single_cell_lps_panels

p_lps_panels <- layout_lps |>
  filter(component == cells_of_interest[1]) |>
  pivot_longer(
    all_of(c(markers_to_viz, "coloc")),
    names_to = "score_type",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  cell_plot(color = score, size = 0.6) |>
  cell_grid(cols = score_type) |>
  cell_node_scale_color() |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction)

export_plot(filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(cell_type_of_interest, "_", cells_of_interest[1], "_lps_panels.png")), plot = autoplot(p_lps_panels))
```

## 6.8. Multi-cell grid plots

Same scores across multiple cells. Columns are cells, rows are score types, and one color limit keeps a strong score in one cell comparable to the others.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_grid

p_grid <- layout_lps |>
  pivot_longer(
    all_of(c(markers_to_viz, "coloc")),
    names_to = "score_type",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  cell_plot(color = score, size = 0.6) |>
  cell_grid(cols = component, rows = score_type) |>
  # White at 0 so negative scores read blue and positive scores read red
  cell_node_scale_color(colors = c("blue", "white", "red"), limits = c(-1, 1)) |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction)

export_plot(filename = file.path(out_dir, paste0(cell_type_of_interest, "_", cells_of_interest[1], "_grid.png")), plot = autoplot(p_grid))
```

## 6.9. Interactive 3D plots

It is possible to create interactive 3D plots of one or multiple cells by feeding a `cell_plot` recipe into `cell_plot_interactive()`. This function than creates a Plotly view, that for example can be embedded in an HTML report.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_interactive
#| eval: false

layout_counts |>
  filter(component == cells_of_interest[1]) |>
  mutate(marker = if_else(marker %in% markers_to_viz, marker, "Other")) |>
  cell_plot(color = marker, size = 1.2, alpha = 1) |>
  cell_node_scale_color(colors = marker_colors) |>
  cell_plot_interactive()
```

This also works for grids of cells.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_rgl
#| eval: false

# Drag any panel to rotate all of them together.
p_grid |> cell_plot_interactive()
```

## 6.10. Animations

We can also create animations of the cell plots. Here, it can be usefule to set `lock_light = TRUE` to keep the highlight fixed to the viewer while the cell turns.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_animate_single
#| eval: false

layout_lps |>
  filter(component == cells_of_interest[1]) |>
  cell_plot(color = coloc, size = 0.7) |>
  cell_node_scale_color() |>
  cell_illuminate(light_direction = light_direction, lock_light = TRUE) |>
  cell_coord_rotate(axis = "y", max_degree = 360) |>
  cell_plot_animate(
    file = file.path(out_dir, paste0(cell_type_of_interest, "_", cells_of_interest[1], "_rotation.gif")),
    frames = 120,
    fps = 20,
    width = 500,
    height = 500
  )
```

And again, this also works for grids of cells. Here we visualize a short "boomerang" motion so each panel moves only a short distance around its own centroid instead of spinning through a full turn.

```{r}
#| label: cell_viz_animate_grid
#| eval: false

p_grid |>
  cell_coord_rotate(axis = "y", max_degree = 30) |>
  cell_plot_animate(
    file = file.path(out_dir, paste0(cell_type_of_interest, "_grid_rotation.gif")),
    frames = 30,
    fps = 15,
    boomerang = TRUE,
    width = 300 * length(cells_of_interest),
    height = 300 * (length(markers_to_viz) + 1)
  )
```
